name: Metoposcopy

card.summary: The historical art of reading character and fortune from forehead lines, an early strand of face-reading.
card.note: Described by dermatology historians as a pseudoscience that is no longer practised.

quick.overview:
Metoposcopy claims that lines and marks on the forehead reveal personality and the future. It is part of a family of face-reading traditions including physiognomy and phrenology.

In looks culture it matters as a historical root of the idea that facial features signal character. It was popularised in the Renaissance by Girolamo Cardano.
quick.how: Practitioners read the pattern of forehead lines and marks and linked them to temperament and destiny.
quick.risks: No physical risk; a 2024 Clinics in Dermatology article calls it a largely forgotten pseudoscience, and it was denounced by Jean Bodin and banned by Pope Sixtus V in 1586.

lead: Metoposcopy is the divinatory interpretation of forehead lines to read character and predict events. The 2024 Clinics in Dermatology article describes it as a skin-based pseudoscience related to palmistry and phrenology [1].

Classical writers mention practitioners, including a metoposcopos cited by Pliny the Elder [2]. Girolamo Cardano wrote Metoposcopia in 1558, published posthumously in 1658, with engravings of 800 foreheads [2].

The practice peaked in the 16th and 17th centuries; Jean Bodin attacked it in 1580 and Pope Sixtus V banned it in 1586 [2]. Historians in medical journals have written on its priority disputes and its link to facial expression studies [1].

chain: Character and fortune inferred from them
Face seen as readable for traits
angle.text: It is a historical belief that the forehead conveys personality. It does not change appearance.

paras: Classical authors mention practitioners, and it appears in Kabbalistic tradition, where Isaac Luria reportedly read Hebrew letters on the forehead [2]. The 2024 article credits ancient Chinese practice and Renaissance popularisation by Cardano [1].
Bodin denounced the art in 1580 and Sixtus V banned it in 1586 [2]. It is no longer practised, unlike palmistry [1].
